posts.title: How one hand pump changed the school day for 200 children
posts.excerpt: Before the pump, the morning walk for water took two hours. Now the classroom fills up before the first bell. Here is what changed, and what is next.
posts.imageAlt: Children filling bottles at a new hand pump

content.text: Every morning, before the sun cleared the ridge, the children of Rampur set out with empty containers. The nearest safe water was a two-hour round trip away, and school simply came second.
The walk that took the morning
Teachers told us attendance dropped every dry season. Children arrived late, tired, or not at all. Parents did not want it that way, but the household still needed water.
I used to carry water before I carried books. Now I carry only my books.
What we built
In March, our field team and local volunteers installed a deep-bore hand pump beside the school. The village council chose the site, and a committee of parents now looks after the maintenance.

items: One deep-bore pump with a protected platform
Two filtration units for the school kitchen
A five-person village committee trained for repairs

content.alt: The new hand pump beside the school
content.caption: The pump sits at the edge of the school yard, where everyone can reach it.

content.text: What is next
Rampur is one of 48 villages we serve. Our next goal is to bring the same safe water to four neighbouring villages before the next dry season begins.

posts.title: Our mobile clinic reaches its 1,000th patient
posts.excerpt: What began as one van and one nurse now visits eleven villages every month. A look back at the first thousand check-ups.
posts.imageAlt: A nurse greeting a patient outside the mobile clinic

content.text: Last Thursday a retired farmer named Gopal stepped into our van for a blood pressure check. He became our one thousandth patient, and he had not seen a doctor in nine years.
Where we started
The clinic began with a single van, a borrowed scale and one nurse. Today it carries a doctor, two nurses, basic diagnostics and a small pharmacy.
People do not ignore their health. They ignore the journey to a hospital.
By bringing check-ups to the village square, we have found conditions early that would otherwise have gone unseen for years.

posts.title: Meet the volunteers rebuilding the Rampur library
posts.excerpt: Twelve volunteers, three weekends and a lot of paint. How a village library came back to life.
posts.imageAlt: Volunteers painting shelves in a village library

content.text: The Rampur library had been closed for six years. The roof leaked, the shelves had collapsed, and the books were stacked in a damp corner.
Twelve people, three weekends
Volunteers from Delhi and the village itself repaired the roof, repainted the walls and built new shelves from reclaimed wood.
Nobody asked us to do it. We just saw it, and it felt wrong to walk past.
